notes: Procedural adjournment only; psychiatric evidence and strike-off context are clearly recorded.

enrichment.short_title: Dutton v Law Society: adjournment of solicitor strike-off appeal
key_facts: Mr Dutton appealed in person against a Solicitors' Disciplinary Tribunal order of 20 February 2003 striking him off the roll for two findings of dishonesty.
He renewed an application for adjournment supported by a consultant psychiatrist's letter of 5 October 2004.
The court spoke to Dr Vaughan by telephone; the doctor confirmed depression but said finalising the appeal today might also be in Mr Dutton's interest.
Mr Goodwin for the Law Society was neutral on the adjournment application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal to the Administrative Court against a Solicitors' Disciplinary Tribunal strike-off order; interlocutory application for adjournment.
enrichment.outcome: The court granted a three-month adjournment with a one-day time estimate on the first open day thereafter, but made clear that no further adjournment would be permitted absent wholly new facts.
enrichment.ratio: Even where the medical basis for adjourning a grave professional discipline appeal is thin, the court may allow one further opportunity to present the case with legal assistance; proceedings cannot continue on an open-ended basis and finality must be balanced against a litigant's ability to do himself justice.
legal_issues: Whether psychiatric evidence justified adjourning the strike-off appeal
How to balance finality in disciplinary proceedings against an unrepresented appellant's capacity to present his case
Whether any further adjournment should be permitted

notes: Offensive weapon reasonable excuse analysis is detailed; Densu distinguished clearly.

enrichment.short_title: DPP v Patterson: reasonable excuse for butterfly knife in public
key_facts: Philip Patterson was charged with possessing an offensive weapon in a public place after police found a butterfly knife on him in a shopping precinct.
Magistrates accepted he intended to leave the knife at his father's shop, then visit his girlfriend and use it to open feed and bedding for horses.
A butterfly knife is an offensive weapon per se under DPP v Hynde.
The DPP appealed by case stated, arguing the magistrates erred in finding a reasonable excuse and in distinguishing R v Densu.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by way of case stated against magistrates' acquittal on a section 1 Prevention of Crime Act 1953 charge.
enrichment.outcome: The appeal was dismissed; the magistrates were entitled to find a reasonable excuse on the facts despite the heavy burden where a weapon is offensive per se.
enrichment.ratio: Reasonable excuse under section 1(1) is of wide purport and is a matter for the fact-finder; Densu's ratio concerned lack of knowledge of offensiveness, not a rule that innocent-purpose explanations can never amount to a reasonable excuse for weapons per se.
legal_issues: Whether carrying a butterfly knife to prepare horse feed could be a reasonable excuse
Whether Densu precludes innocent-purpose defences for weapons offensive per se
Whether the magistrates' factual findings were open to them

notes: Long POCA civil recovery judgment; section 308 construction and non-disclosure analysis are thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Assets Recovery Agency v Singh: civil recovery after quashed confiscation
key_facts: Mr Singh pleaded guilty to conspiracy to cheat the public revenue over a diversion fraud and was sentenced in 1998; a confiscation order of £300,000 was later quashed on appeal in December 2002 for procedural defects.
After the restraint order was discharged, Customs released seized cash to his solicitors in March 2003, shortly after the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 came into force.
The Assets Recovery Agency obtained an interim receiving order without notice in April 2003 and later issued civil recovery proceedings over the same assets.
Singh applied to strike out the claim and discharge the IRO, arguing section 308(9) excluded the property and that there had been material non-disclosure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application to strike out civil recovery proceedings and discharge an interim receiving order under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.
enrichment.outcome: Both applications were dismissed; section 308(9) applies only to extant confiscation orders, section 308(1) did not protect unpaid solicitors' fees, Article 6 was not breached, and material non-disclosure did not warrant discharge of the IRO.
enrichment.ratio: Property taken into account in a confiscation hearing is not excluded from civil recovery under section 308(9) once that order has been quashed and is null for future purposes; the civil recovery regime may proceed despite prior criminal proceedings, and innocent non-disclosure by a referring authority does not automatically vitiate a without-notice order where merits and balance of convenience favour retention.
legal_issues: Whether assets previously assessed in quashed confiscation proceedings were recoverable property
Whether solicitors' unpaid fees were protected by section 308(1)
Whether cumulative delay breached Article 6
Whether non-disclosure of Customs correspondence justified discharging the interim receiving order

enrichment.short_title: Lewis v King: internet libel and forum conveniens
key_facts: Don King sued Lennox Lewis's attorney Judd Burstein for libel over website articles accusing King of antisemitism, published in California but downloaded in England.
King discontinued against Lewis and Lion, leaving Burstein as sole defendant.
Eady J upheld Master Whittaker's order permitting service out of the jurisdiction.
Burstein argued New York was the appropriate forum and that the judge wrongly treated King's inability to sue there under New York Times v Sullivan as a juridical advantage.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal challenge to refusal to set aside permission to serve a libel claim form out of the jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Eady J did not err in treating England as the clearly appropriate forum and did not impermissibly rely on juridical advantage.
enrichment.ratio: In internet defamation cases the court retains a broad discretion on forum conveniens, but must not treat a claimant's inability to obtain relief abroad as a reason to permit English proceedings at the first stage of the Spiliada analysis; publication where downloaded remains the starting point, though global publication and the publisher's choice of a ubiquitous medium inform the exercise of discretion.
legal_issues: Whether Eady J erred by treating New York Times v Sullivan as a juridical advantage
How forum conveniens principles apply to internet libel
Whether defendant targeting of jurisdictions should be considered
Whether witness location difficulties disclosed an error of law

notes: Major HGCRA adjudication enforcement ruling; complexity and natural justice issues comprehensively resolved.

enrichment.short_title: CIB v Birse: enforcing complex construction adjudication award

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: CIB terminated Birse's main contract for the Riverdale Data Centre and later demanded about £16.6 million for completion costs and related claims.
After mediation and tactical correspondence, CIB referred the dispute to adjudication in November 2003; John Uff QC awarded CIB £2,164,892 in February 2004.
Birse resisted enforcement on grounds including lack of a crystallised dispute, pre-adjudication unfairness, procedural unfairness, excessive complexity, and an alleged slip on cladding defects.
Adjudication costs exceeded £2.1 million excluding VAT, with over 100 lever-arch files of documents.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court application to enforce an adjudicator's decision under section 108 of the HGCRA 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Enforcement ordered; the dispute had crystallised, Birse was not ambushed, the adjudicator acted fairly within agreed extensions, complexity did not invalidate adjudication, and the alleged slip was not a correctable accidental error.
enrichment.ratio: A party has a general right to refer any construction dispute to adjudication irrespective of complexity, but enforcement depends on whether the adjudicator reached a fair decision within the time limits agreed under section 108(2); tactical pre-referral manoeuvring and piecemeal extensions do not automatically render the process unfair if both parties participated and the adjudicator gave a proper opportunity to present the case.
legal_issues: Whether a dispute had crystallised before the notice of adjudication
Whether CIB's conduct rendered the adjudication irredeemably unfair
Whether the dispute was too complex for adjudication
Whether the adjudicator made a slip warranting non-enforcement

notes: Driving whilst disqualified case; Scott v Jelf and section 101 burden analysis are clear.

enrichment.short_title: DPP v Barker: burden of proving provisional licence exemption
key_facts: Martin Barker was seen driving while still disqualified until passing an extended test after an earlier 12-month disqualification had expired.
Magistrates acquitted him because the prosecution did not prove he lacked a provisional licence, L plates, or a qualified supervising driver.
The prosecution relied on his interview admission that he had no authority to drive.
The DPP appealed by case stated on the burden of proof under section 37(3).
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by way of case stated against magistrates' acquittal on a driving whilst disqualified charge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed with a direction to convict; the defendant bore the burden of proving he drove in accordance with a provisional licence under section 37(3) and section 101 of the Magistrates' Courts Act 1980.
enrichment.ratio: Section 37(3) gives a disqualified driver a limited exemption only if he holds a provisional licence and drives in accordance with its conditions; breach of those conditions removes the protection and the exemption must be proved by the defendant.
legal_issues: Whether the prosecution had to disprove compliance with provisional licence conditions
Whether section 101 applied to the section 37(3) exemption
Whether Scott v Jelf governed the construction of section 37(3)

notes: Employment Appeal Tribunal review decision restored; Ladd v Marshall analysis applied.

enrichment.short_title: Walker v Barnes: employment tribunal review of new evidence
key_facts: Mr Barnes, treated as self-employed for six years, was found to have been an employee and unfairly dismissed by Walker's Windows for allegedly diverting work to Cavanagh Construction.
The employment tribunal found no systematic fraud but applied a 30% contributory conduct reduction.
Walker's later review application relied on a further Cavanagh garage conversion job as new evidence under rule 13.
The Employment Appeal Tribunal remitted for reconsideration of contribution, but the Court of Appeal restored the tribunal chairman's refusal to review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal against an Employment Appeal Tribunal decision remitting contributory conduct for rehearing after a refused tribunal review.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the chairman's decision refusing review was not perverse and the new evidence would not have had an important influence on the 30% contribution finding.
enrichment.ratio: An employment tribunal chairman applying Ladd v Marshall is entitled to refuse review where fresh evidence is merely cumulative of earlier Cavanagh-related incidents and would not materially affect contributory conduct; the Employment Appeal Tribunal cannot treat that evaluative judgment as perverse simply because the new evidence might have cast some doubt on the employee's explanation.
legal_issues: Whether the garage conversion evidence passed the Ladd v Marshall test
Whether the Employment Appeal Tribunal erred in treating the chairman's decision as perverse
Whether remittal for rehearing was appropriate
linked_authorities: Ladd v Marshall [1954] 1 WLR 1489

notes: Landmark Hague Convention Article 12(2) settlement appeal; Singer J's departures rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Cannon v Cannon: Hague Convention settlement and return discretion
key_facts: A mother twice abducted her daughter from California to the British Isles, concealing their identities for over four years after a consent return order in 1999.
Proceedings were commenced more than one year after the second abduction; the father sought return under the Hague Convention.
Singer J held the child was settled under Article 12(2) and that no Convention discretion to order return remained.
The Court of Appeal restored the established UK approach requiring physical and emotional settlement and retaining Article 18 discretion.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a reserved High Court judgment on the meaning of Article 12(2) settlement and the effect of Article 18 in Hague Convention return proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on both issues; settlement requires physical and emotional elements, concealment increases the burden of proof, and even if settlement is proved the court retains a residual discretion under Article 18 to order return; case remitted.
enrichment.ratio: Article 12(2) settlement is not satisfied by physical presence alone but includes emotional and psychological stability; concealment and subterfuge critically undermine settlement, and Article 18 preserves a Convention discretion to order return even after settlement is established.
legal_issues: What degree of settlement Article 12(2) requires
Whether concealment prevents or tolls the one-year period
Whether a finding of settlement removes Convention jurisdiction to order return
How Article 18 interacts with Article 12(2)

notes: Asylum judicial review; Tharmakulaseelan release reasoning upheld on full merits review.

enrichment.short_title: Sunderalingam v IAT: Sri Lankan asylum risk on return

statutes_considered.title: Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms 1950

key_facts: A Tamil appellant fled Sri Lanka after deserting the LTTE, army detention, torture, and release following a bribe.
The adjudicator accepted much of his history but found no continuing adverse record or real risk of persecution on return, applying Tharmakulaseelan.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused permission to appeal, stating release after a bribe meant no adverse record.
Sedley LJ granted permission to challenge the refusal as a possible non sequitur; the Court of Appeal heard the matter as a substantive judicial review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal judicial review of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal of permission to appeal against an asylum adjudicator's dismissal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; even assuming the IAT decision was flawed, the underlying grounds had no real prospect of success because the adjudicator properly applied Tharmakulaseelan and assessed risk on the specific facts.
enrichment.ratio: Where an adjudicator finds release from army custody after a bribe did not create a continuing adverse record or interest, that conclusion is consistent with Tharmakulaseelan; a compressed IAT refusal reason is not a non sequitur if read in context, and judicial review may still be refused where no real prospect of success exists on the substantive grounds.
legal_issues: Whether release after bribery meant no adverse record
Whether the brother-in-law's detention created a real risk on return
Whether the IAT Vice-President's reasoning contained a non sequitur
Whether UNHCR material was properly considered
linked_authorities: Tharmakulaseelan v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2002] UKIAT 03444

notes: Restricted road order construction under section 82(2)(b) resolved clearly against respondent.

enrichment.short_title: DPP v Evans: section 82(2)(b) restricted road orders
key_facts: Ms Evans was prosecuted for exceeding 30 mph on the B4551, relying on Worcestershire County Council restricted road orders made in February 2002.
The relevant stretches lacked street lighting under section 82(1) but had repeater 30 mph signs.
The district judge held section 82(2)(b) could not make an unlit road a restricted road and that section 84(1) was the only route to a 30 mph limit.
The DPP appealed by case stated, arguing section 82(2)(b) plainly authorises such orders.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by way of case stated against dismissal of a speeding prosecution for invalid restricted road orders.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the orders were lawful, section 82(2)(b) means what it says, and any tension with Direction 10 of the Traffic Signs Regulations does not defeat the statutory power.
enrichment.ratio: Section 82(2)(b) empowers a traffic authority to direct that a road which is not a restricted road under section 82(1) shall become one and thereby attract the 30 mph limit in section 81(1); the power is not limited to reversing an earlier de-restriction and overlaps with section 84(1) without rendering either otiose.
legal_issues: Whether section 82(2)(b) applies to roads without section 82(1) street lighting
Whether the power is confined to reversing section 82(2)(a) de-restrictions
Whether Direction 10 inconsistency invalidates restricted road orders on unlit roads
linked_authorities: Harrods Ltd v Remick [1998] 1 All ER 52
